One of the players leads the trick by playing a card and everyone must follow suit. Whoever played the highest card wins the trick and chooses one of the played cards to put in the stock portfolio. All cards have shares, which yield victory points according to the companies' market value. Some cards, when used, allow the player to modify a company's stock exchange rate, either in his favor or to ruin opponents' dreams. Number of players: 2 - 5 Game duration: 16 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Stonks and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Setup 3 Turn 4 Stock Market 5 Speculation 6 Round End 7 Game End Overview Have the most profitable stocks in your portfolio by game's end Setup Each player starts by picking two cards to add to their portfolio, one visible and one hidden. Each of those cards gives the player one stock per suit icon in that company; these stocks will score the player points at the end of the round. The player with the lowest visible card will start the round, with ties being split in favour of the lowest starting share value. Turn This is a trick taking game. At the start of each trick the top card of the deck is revealed - this can be claimed by the person who wins the trick, it desired. The starting player (or whoever won the last trick) plays a card, and all subsequent players (clockwise) must play a card of the matching suit. If unable, they can play any card or a trump card - the trump suit is the current company with the lowest market value. If a player plays a card with the Stock Market symbol (a set of two arrows) then they also get to adjust the Stock Market as discussed below. The player with the highest value card in the starting suit wins the trick, unless a trump was played in which case the highest trump card wins. (But see Speculation below.) The winner of the trick chooses one of the played cards or the face-up card which was flipped at the start of the trick, and adds it to their portfolio. They then commence the next trick. Stock Market If a player plays a card with the Stock Market symbol (a set of two arrows) then they also get to adjust a stock in the market by one level up or down at the time of playing (This could change Trump) Some cards have TWO Stock Market symbols, in which case both must be applied to the same company in the same direction, if this would push the company further than allowed (i.e. there is just one space left in that direction) the player has to move in the other direction or pick a different company Whatever company just got changed will gain the black mark, a company with the black mark cannot be adjusted at the next adjustment, at which point the adjusted company will instead gain the black mark (i.e. there will always be one company which cannot be affected, but this will always be changing) Speculation One Speculation card can be played per round, so the first player to play one blocks that option for the remaining players If the starting player plays the speculation, they also place a normal card face down, then card call any company to be the suit for the round At end of round, the facedown card is revealed and scored as normal i.e. if it were the suit called (but doesn't have to be) or perhaps it were the trump suit, it has a chance at winning through highest suit. Any market exchange symbols are forfeited If the facedown card was not from the lead suit, and no one played a suit or trump card, no one wins the trick, the cards are all discarded, and that player starts again If a follower wishes to play the Speculation, they have to have NO Lead suit cards in hand, if this is the case they can play Speculation along with a faceup other card and make it the Lead suit e.g. a Red is lead, a player can play a yellow 13 with a Speculation and call it a red 13 A later player can counter a Follow Speculation by playing the real card, e.g. the real red 13 in the above example, which nullifies the Speculation and returns the card to its original form, a yellow 13 in the example Regardless of how a Specu

[Rating: 1/10] Thematically like Trick & Trade, but very very average. No one really strikes it rich (or poor), or even feels nefariously manipulative. Instead, everyone just fiddles values up and down and adjusts the scoring? Too many rules for such a simple game, it felt oddly complex for how little it's trying to do.

[Rating: 4/10] This was a disappointment. There's a bit too much going on in each trick and it's a bit fiddly in general.  Play Trick of the Rails instead.

[Rating: 4/10] I don't know why anyone would pick this trick-taker over hundreds of others. The economy is a gimmick and there are more strategically-important-but-ultimately-irrelevant rules to understand and keep in your head EVERY trick.

[Rating: 5/10] Really disappointing actually. There's some interesting stuff going on with the way the trump suit can shift during the truck, but most of the cardplay felt really annoying. Trick taking games already have an issue with player agency, but this game exacerbates that by not dealing or like half the deck and making it impossible to do much of anything if you have a bad hand. Really, really disappointing, especially considering all the cool systems that the game had

[Rating: 5/10] This is a trick taking card game with a stock market theme. When a player wins a trick, they get to keep either one of the cards played or one that was revealed on the side. Each suit represents a stock in a company. Some of the cards represent two stocks, and low value cards typically allow you to manipulate the value of the stocks. What makes this different than most trick taking games is the trump suit is the company with the lowest value, so the trump can change midway through a hand if company values were adjusted. [Rating: 5/10] Too lucky for what it is trying to do. Since you only earn stocks (points) on tricks you win, a bad hand really does nothing for you aside from maybe making the amount of points other players scoop up lower. An interesting concept that just didn't work for me, but might be interesting if you don't mind as much luck in your trick takers.

[Rating: 5/10] Rating based on 3 plays on BGA.  As a huge fan of trick-taking games, there are some interesting concepts at play here - the stock-market fluctuation that determines trump, the price manipulation through lower cards, the hidden cards, and bluffing of speculation. However, the whole thing just doesn't work for me.  Not enough tricks in a round. The speculation is too easy to manipulate. The price fluctuations don't change enough, and there's not a lot you can do to mitigate a strong hand.  I also dislike that style of artwork.  Not one I enjoyed or would recommend.
